description: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is a culinary masterpiece from Oaxaca, Mexico, renowned for its incredible depth and complexity of flavor. This traditional sauce boasts a rich, dark hue and a symphony of tastes, blending various chiles, spices, nuts, seeds, and a hint of Mexican chocolate. It's a true labor of love, perfect for special occasions and a testament to the vibrant heritage of Mexican cuisine.

instructions.title: Prepare and Rehydrate Chiles
instructions.text: Lightly toast the dried Pasilla Oaxaca, Mulato, Ancho, and Chipotle chiles on a comal or dry skillet over medium heat for 30 seconds per side until fragrant. Be careful not to burn them, as this will make the mole bitter. Immediately transfer the toasted chiles to a bowl and cover with very hot water. Let them soak for 20-30 minutes until softened, then drain and set aside, reserving some soaking liquid.

instructions.title: Roast Aromatics and Vegetables
instructions.text: While the chiles rehydrate, roast the tomatillos, Roma tomatoes, roughly chopped onion, and peeled garlic cloves on the comal or a baking sheet until softened and slightly charred, about 10-15 minutes. Set aside.

instructions.title: Fry Nuts, Seeds, and Spices
instructions.text: In a separate skillet, heat 1 tablespoon of lard or oil over medium heat. Fry the sliced plantain until golden brown, then remove and set aside. In the same skillet, add the raisins, almonds, pecans, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, cinnamon stick, whole cloves, and black peppercorns. Toast them gently, stirring constantly, for 3-5 minutes until fragrant and lightly golden. Be careful not to burn the sesame seeds.

instructions.title: Blend the Mole Base
instructions.text: Combine the rehydrated chiles, roasted tomatillos, tomatoes, onion, garlic, fried plantain, toasted nuts, seeds, and spices in a blender. Add the Mexican oregano, dried thyme, and ground cumin. Pour in 2 cups of hot chicken broth and blend until the mixture is as smooth as possible. This may take several minutes. If needed, add a little more chicken broth or reserved chile soaking liquid to help the blending process, but use sparingly. Strain the blended mixture through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl, pressing firmly on the solids with the back of a spoon to extract all the liquid. Discard the solids.

instructions.title: Cook the Mole Sauce
instructions.text: Heat the remaining 3 tablespoons of lard or oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat until shimmering. Carefully pour the strained mole sauce into the hot fat. Be prepared for it to splatter. Cook, stirring constantly, for at least 20-30 minutes. This step is crucial for developing the mole's deep flavor and rich color; the sauce will thicken and darken significantly.

instructions.title: Finish and Serve the Mole
instructions.text: Stir in the Mexican chocolate until it melts completely and is fully incorporated into the sauce. Gradually add 4-6 more cups of hot chicken broth, or until the mole reaches your desired consistency. It should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Season with salt to taste, and add the teaspoon of sugar if you find the flavors need a little balancing. Reduce the heat to low and simmer gently for at least 30-45 minutes, stirring occasionally, to allow all the flavors to meld beautifully. Serve the Mole Negro hot over cooked chicken pieces, garnished with extra toasted sesame seeds. Enjoy this Oaxacan treasure!

tips: Toasting chiles properly is key: just until fragrant, not burnt. Burnt chiles will make the mole bitter.
For an extra rich flavor, toast the nuts and seeds in a small amount of lard or oil before blending.
The straining step is essential for a smooth, velvety mole. Don't rush it; press thoroughly to extract all the flavor.
Mole Negro improves with age. Make it a day ahead and gently reheat for even deeper flavors.
article:
## Unveiling the Mystique of Mole Negro: An Authentic Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe

Deep within the heart of Mexico, in the vibrant state of Oaxaca, lies a culinary tradition that tells stories of ancient civilizations, diverse landscapes, and generations of passionate cooks. Among its revered "seven moles," none commands as much awe and admiration as Mole Negro, or Oaxacan Black Mole. This isn't just a sauce; it's a symphony of flavors, a labor of love, and a testament to the sophisticated culinary heritage of Mexico. If you're looking for an authentic and deeply satisfying Mexican dinner recipe, the Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe is a culinary journey worth embarking on.

Often reserved for special occasions like weddings, baptisms, and major holidays, Mole Negro is a dish of profound complexity and unparalleled depth. Its iconic dark hue hints at the rich tapestry of ingredients within, promising an experience that transcends the ordinary. Preparing it is a ritual, a patient layering of flavors that culminates in a sauce so profound it can transform a simple piece of chicken into an extraordinary feast.

## What is Oaxacan Black Mole (Mole Negro)?

Oaxacan Black Mole, or Mole Negro, is widely considered the king of moles, originating from Oaxaca, often called "The Land of Seven Moles." Unlike simpler moles, Mole Negro is distinguished by its intensely dark color, achieved through the careful roasting and charring of multiple types of chiles and other ingredients. Its flavor profile is a complex dance between smoky, sweet, spicy, earthy, and savory notes, with hints of fruit, nuts, and chocolate.

The creation of Mole Negro is an art form passed down through generations. It involves a meticulous process of toasting, grinding, frying, and simmering over 20, and sometimes up to 30 or more, distinct ingredients. Key components typically include several varieties of dried chiles (especially the rare chilhuacle negro), nuts, seeds, spices, fruits, vegetables, and the crucial addition of Mexican chocolate. The result is a thick, velvety sauce that clings beautifully to poultry or pork, offering a taste experience that is both ancient and utterly modern. While intimidating to some, mastering the Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe is a rewarding experience that connects you directly to the heart of Mexican cuisine.

## Ingredients for Authentic Mole Negro

Before diving into the Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe, gathering the right ingredients is paramount. Quality and authenticity will significantly impact the final flavor. This list focuses on traditional components, but some substitutions can be made if certain chiles are unavailable.

**The Chiles (essential for color and flavor):**
*   4-6 large Mulato chiles
*   4-6 large Ancho chiles
*   4-6 large Pasilla Oaxaca chiles (or Pasilla Negro if Oaxaca not available)
*   4-6 Chilhuacle Negro chiles (highly recommended for authenticity, but rare; if unavailable, increase other dark chiles)
*   1-2 Chipotle chiles (for a smoky kick)

**Aromatics & Vegetables:**
*   1 medium white onion, roughly chopped
*   6-8 cloves garlic, peeled
*   2 medium ripe tomatoes, roughly chopped
*   2 medium tomatillos, husked and roughly chopped
*   1 plantain, ripe (yellow with black spots), sliced
*   1/2 cup raisins

**Nuts, Seeds & Thickeners:**
*   1/2 cup almonds
*   1/2 cup peanuts
*   1/4 cup sesame seeds (plus more for garnish)
*   1/4 cup pumpkin seeds (pepitas)
*   2-3 stale corn tortillas or 1 slice of stale bread (bolillo or baguette)

**Spices (whole spices are best):**
*   1 cinnamon stick (about 3 inches)
*   6-8 whole cloves
*   1 teaspoon whole black peppercorns
*   1/2 teaspoon cumin seeds
*   1/4 teaspoon anise seeds (optional)
*   1/2 teaspoon dried thyme
*   1/2 teaspoon dried oregano (Mexican oregano if possible)

**The Sweet & Savory Finish:**
*   1-2 tablets (about 3-4 oz) authentic Mexican chocolate (e.g., Ibarra or Abuelita), roughly chopped
*   2-3 tablespoons piloncillo (Mexican brown sugar cone) or dark brown sugar, to taste
*   1/2 cup lard or vegetable oil, divided
*   6-8 cups chicken broth (or vegetable broth for a vegetarian version), plus more if needed
*   Salt to taste

## Step-by-Step Instructions to Make Black Mole

This detailed Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe requires patience and several stages, but the reward is immense.

**1. Prepare the Chiles:**
*   Carefully remove stems and seeds from all dried chiles. For a spicier mole, leave a few seeds in.
*   Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium-low heat. Toast the chiles one by one, pressing them down with tongs, until aromatic and slightly pliable, about 30 seconds per side. Be careful not to burn them, as this will make the mole bitter.
*   Once toasted, place the chiles in a large bowl and cover them with very hot water. Let them rehydrate for at least 20-30 minutes, until soft.

**2. Toast Nuts, Seeds, and Spices:**
*   In the same dry skillet, toast the sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds, almonds, and peanuts separately until lightly golden and fragrant. Set aside.
*   Toast the cinnamon stick, cloves, peppercorns, cumin seeds, and anise seeds (if using) until aromatic, about 1-2 minutes. Set aside.

**3. Fry Aromatics and Thickeners:**
*   Heat about 2 tablespoons of lard or oil in a large skillet or Dutch oven over medium heat.
*   Fry the chopped onion and garlic until softened and lightly browned. Remove and set aside.
*   Add a bit more oil if needed, then fry the tomatoes and tomatillos until softened and slightly charred. Remove and set aside.
*   Fry the sliced plantain until golden brown. Remove and set aside.
*   Fry the raisins until plump. Remove and set aside.
*   Briefly fry the stale tortillas or bread until golden and crisp. Remove and set aside.

**4. Blend the Ingredients (The Heart of the Mole):**
*   Drain the rehydrated chiles, reserving about 1 cup of the soaking liquid.
*   In batches, blend all the toasted chiles, fried aromatics (onion, garlic, tomatoes, tomatillos), fried plantain, raisins, toasted nuts, seeds, and spices, along with the fried tortillas/bread.
*   Add chicken broth and some of the reserved chile soaking liquid as needed to create a very smooth, thick paste. Blend thoroughly. If your blender isn't powerful enough, you may need to pass the paste through a fine-mesh sieve or food mill after blending to achieve a silky texture.

**5. Cook the Mole:**
*   Heat the remaining lard or oil (about 1/4 cup) in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium heat. This step is crucial for developing the mole's deep flavor.
*   Carefully pour the blended mole paste into the hot lard. It will splatter, so use caution.
*   Stir constantly with a wooden spoon for at least 20-30 minutes. This frying process "cooks out" the raw flavor of the chiles and deepens the overall taste. The mole will darken further and thicken, pulling away from the sides of the pot.
*   Gradually add the chicken broth, about 1 cup at a time, stirring continuously to incorporate.
*   Add the chopped Mexican chocolate and piloncillo/brown sugar. Stir until dissolved.
*   Bring the mole to a gentle simmer. Reduce heat to low, cover partially, and cook for at least 1-2 hours, stirring frequently to prevent sticking and burning. The longer it simmers, the more the flavors meld and deepen. Add more broth if the mole becomes too thick; it should have a consistency like a thick gravy.
*   Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and more piloncillo/sugar if needed. The mole should be a harmonious balance of sweet, savory, and spicy.

## Pro Tips for the Best Oaxacan Black Mole

*   **Don't Rush the Toasting:** Each ingredient plays a crucial role. Toasting chiles carefully (not burning!) and bringing out the oils in nuts and seeds is vital for flavor.
*   **Quality Chiles:** If you can find Chilhuacle Negro chiles, they are worth the effort for an authentic Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe. Otherwise, use a good mix of mulato, ancho, and pasilla Oaxaca.
*   **Mexican Chocolate is Key:** It contains cinnamon and other spices that are integral to the mole's flavor. Don't substitute with regular baking chocolate unless absolutely necessary.
*   **Blend, Blend, Blend:** A powerful blender is your best friend. For the smoothest mole, consider straining the finished paste through a fine-mesh sieve.
*   **Patience in Cooking:** The long simmering time is non-negotiable. It allows the complex flavors to meld and deepen, transforming the paste into a rich, cohesive sauce.
*   **Make Ahead:** Mole is one of those dishes that tastes even better the next day, after the flavors have had more time to marry. It also freezes beautifully.
*   **Season Gradually:** Taste frequently as you simmer and adjust salt and sweetness. The balance is critical.

## Serving Suggestions for Mole Negro

The traditional Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe is often served with simply cooked proteins, allowing the mole to be the star.

*   **Classic Pairing:** Ladle generously over tender pieces of cooked chicken or turkey (poached, roasted, or braised).
*   **Other Proteins:** It also pairs wonderfully with pork (pork loin or carnitas), duck, or even beef short ribs.
*   **Vegetarian Options:** For a plant-based meal, serve over roasted sweet potatoes, grilled portobello mushrooms, or cheese enchiladas. It's also delicious with tamales.
*   **Accompaniments:** Always serve with warm corn tortillas for scooping up every last drop. A side of fluffy Mexican red rice and simple black beans completes the authentic experience.
*   **Garnish:** A sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds and perhaps a little fresh cilantro adds a lovely touch.

## Variations and Substitutions

While the Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe is quite specific, there's always room for personal touch and adaptation based on ingredient availability.

*   **Chiles:** If Chilhuacle Negro chiles are impossible to find, increase the quantity of Mulato and Ancho chiles to compensate for the depth of flavor and color.
*   **Nuts/Seeds:** You can adjust the ratio of almonds, peanuts, sesame, and pumpkin seeds based on preference or what you have on hand. Cashews can also be added for richness.
*   **Thickeners:** Instead of tortillas or bread, you can use a small amount of masa harina (corn flour) dissolved in water, added towards the end of cooking, though it slightly alters the texture.
*   **Sweetener:** If piloncillo isn't available, dark brown sugar is the best substitute. Start with less and add to taste.
*   **Vegetarian/Vegan:** Use vegetable broth instead of chicken broth. For frying, opt for a neutral vegetable oil instead of lard. Serve with hearty vegetables or plant-based proteins.
*   **Exploring Other Moles:** This Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe is just one of many incredible moles. Once you've mastered this, you might explore Mole Rojo (red mole), Mole Verde (green mole), or Mole Amarillo (yellow mole), each with its own unique flavor profile and ingredient list, showcasing the incredible diversity of Mexican dinner recipes.

Embrace the journey of creating this magnificent dish. The Oaxacan Black Mole Recipe is more than just food; it's a celebration of culture, history, and the profound joy of sharing a truly extraordinary meal.
